demand.reason: Global terbium consumption is estimated on the order of 400–600 metric tons annually, crossing into the modest-demand band of 500–10,000 tons.

growth.reason: Terbium demand is driven almost entirely by its role as a co-dopant in high-performance NdFeB permanent magnets for electric vehicle traction motors and direct-drive wind turbines. The projected exponential expansion of the global EV fleet mandates high-temperature magnetic coercivity, securing a high-growth trajectory well exceeding 12% CAGR.

supplier_concentration.reason:
Mining: China controls approximately 70% of global heavy rare earth mining, including vital feedstock from Myanmar that directly supplies Chinese processing hubs, placing primary mining concentration in the 65–85% band (Score 4).


Refining: China dominates the entire downstream value chain, controlling over 90% of global heavy rare earth refining capacity. This near-monopoly exceeds the 85% threshold, placing refining diversity at the highly concentrated maximum (Score 5).

reserves.reason:
Time-frame: Terbium is primarily sourced from surficial ion-adsorption clay deposits. The most economical horizons face rapid depletion under intense extraction rates, pacing the viable reserve lifespan for low-cost production at 30–50 years, matching Score 3.


Diversification: Economically productive ion-adsorption clay deposits are overwhelmingly concentrated in southern China and Myanmar. Because a single nation controls nearly 100% of these specialized heavy rare earth reserves, the resulting HHI is >0.60 (Score 5).

end_use.reason:
Defense & National Security (+1.5): NdFeB magnets containing terbium are foundational to military electric drive systems, submarine propulsion, and smart munition actuators. Energy Generation & Grid (+1.5): direct-drive offshore wind turbines utilize large-mass NdFeB generators requiring high terbium content. Electrification & Transport (+1.0): required for high-temperature EV traction motors via grain boundary diffusion. Healthcare & Biomedical (+1.0): acts as a luminescent activator in time-resolved fluoroimmunoassay diagnostic reagents.


Sector presence scores total 5.0 across 4 qualifying sectors. The breadth bonus for 4 sectors adds +1.5, yielding an objective composite score of 6.5.

substitutability_recyclability.reason:
Substitutability: Dysprosium can act as a partial co-coercivity substitute, but terbium provides uniquely superior efficiency per gram in grain boundary diffusion. While research into terbium-lean magnets exists, no commercially proven alternative achieves equivalent coercivity at production scale for high-temperature EV and military motors, requiring fundamental redesigns to adopt (Score 4).


Recyclability: Terbium recycling from permanent magnets remains below 5% globally. Terbium constitutes ~0.1–0.3% of magnet mass, making chemical isolation via full hydrometallurgical cascades economically prohibitive compared to primary mining, matching the negligible recycling tier (<5%).

extraction_refining.reason: Heavy rare earth separation represents the absolute frontier of chemical processing difficulty. Extracting terbium requires in-situ leaching followed by 50–80 stages of solvent extraction in counter-current cascades to separate it from near-identical lanthanides (gadolinium, dysprosium). This specialized chemistry is restricted to Chinese facilities, reflecting extreme complexity and nation-state level capability.

upcoming_projects.reason: Following Chinese export controls, committed Western projects like the Mountain Pass separation facility (US) and the Mara Rosa ionic clay project (Brazil) received major funding, but represent early-stage developments with first production slated for 2028–2030. This minimal pipeline offers <5% near-term supply additions with high execution risks.

india_position.reason:
Import Dependence: India possesses coastal monazite deposits processed by IREL, but terbium traces are minute (~0.1–0.3% of REO). India lacks commercial heavy rare earth separation capability, making its burgeoning domestic NdFeB magnet and EV motor industries 100% import-dependent for separated terbium (Score 5).


Strategic Posture: Terbium is listed as a critical mineral, and India actively participates in the Minerals Security Partnership (MSP) and Australia technology working groups. However, KABIL maintains no specific terbium mandate and holds no binding foreign equity stakes, reflecting declared strategic intent at an early stage (Score 3).

price_volatility.reason: Terbium prices are opaque and highly sensitive to trade policies. Following a 38% surge in early 2024, the market experienced extreme disruption when China enacted explicit export controls on heavy rare earths in April 2025. This weaponized supply action triggered severe shortages and price spikes exceeding 100%, causing structural market breakdown and extreme volatility.

capability.name: Terbium
capability.next_move: Recover Tb from magnet scrap; use grain-boundary diffusion to cut Tb per magnet; heavy-REE separation later.
capability.what_india_has: Same base as dysprosium: IREL's pilot separation, magnet recovery at Bhopal, Neyveli ash and new magnet makers.

stages.world: China ~91% of REE separation; Lynas separates heavy REEs in Malaysia since 2025.

stages.india: IREL wants to buy 200 t of Tb oxide.

strategyList.name: Rare-earth separation
strategyList.what: Hundreds of solvent-extraction stages split chemically near-identical rare earths into pure oxides.
strategyList.outside_china: China ~91%. Malaysia (Lynas, heavy REEs since 2025); France (Caremag, 2026); Australia (Iluka, being built).
strategyList.cost: Iluka Eneabba (Australia): A$1.7-1.8 bn for ~17.5 kt/yr of REO, incl. up to ~5.5 kt NdPr and ~0.75 kt Dy/Tb. Caremag (France): EUR 216 m, incl. ~600 t/yr of Dy/Tb oxides.
strategyList.india_base: IREL (light REEs, commercial; heavy REEs at pilot scale); Toyotsu (Vizag); solvent-extraction skills in pharma and chemical firms.

strategyList.name: Rare-earth metal making (metallisation)
strategyList.what: Turning oxides into metal: molten-salt electrolysis for Nd and Pr; calcium reduction of fluorides for Dy, Tb and Gd. The step before alloys and magnets.
strategyList.outside_china: Little capacity outside China; exact shares are not published.
strategyList.cost: India's magnet scheme funds oxide to metal to alloy to magnet: Rs 7,280 crore (Rs 6,450 crore sales incentives + Rs 750 crore capital subsidy) for 6,000 t/yr.
strategyList.india_base: Mini plants for La, Ce and Nd metal at the Bhopal theme park; BARC and DMRL know-how; scheme bidders must include this step.
strategyList.gap: Commercial electrolysis cells; fluoride chemistry for heavy-REE metals.

strategyList.name: Permanent magnet making
strategyList.what: Alloying, strip casting, jet milling, pressing, sintering and coating (NdFeB); reduction-diffusion and sintering (SmCo).
strategyList.outside_china: China 94% of sintered magnets. Outside: Japan and Europe, with new plants such as Neo's in Estonia.
strategyList.cost: Neo (Estonia): over EUR 100 m for 2,000 t/yr, ~EUR 250 m to reach 5,000 t/yr. India's scheme: Rs 7,280 crore for 6,000 t/yr.
strategyList.india_base: IREL's 3 t/yr SmCo plant (Vizag); 20 bids for the magnet scheme (Aug 2026); DMRL and BARC know-how.
strategyList.gap: Scale; equipment; Dy/Tb-saving diffusion; qualification with motor makers.

strategyList.name: Recycling (batteries, magnets, catalysts, PV)
strategyList.what: Shredding and hydrometallurgy of black mass; magnet recovery; spent-catalyst leaching; PV-panel recovery.
strategyList.outside_china: Battery recycling: China has over three-quarters of pre-treatment and 90% of material-recovery capacity; Europe, Japan, Korea and the US smaller.
strategyList.cost: India's scheme expects ~Rs 8,000 crore for 270+ kt/yr of capacity (~Rs 30 crore per kt/yr), yielding ~40 kt/yr of critical minerals.
strategyList.india_base: Lohum, Rubamin, the Bhopal magnet facility, CSIR-NML; Rs 1,500 crore incentive scheme (2025).

chemistryList.name: Fluorochemicals and HF
chemistryList.who: GFCL (India's largest integrated fluoropolymer maker; fluorspar mine in Morocco); Navin Fluorine (AHF project at Dahej).
chemistryList.carries_over_to: LiPF6 electrolyte salt; HF purification of graphite; rare-earth fluorides for metal making; etching chemicals for gallium and silicon devices.
chemistryList.fit: Direct for LiPF6; adjacent for the rest
chemistryList.summary: Fluorine chemistry is a shared industrial foundation for battery salts, selected mineral-purification routes and electronic chemicals. India's existing HF plants provide a starting point, but each application needs its own process, purity controls and customer qualification.

links.how: Rare-earth fluorides are intermediates or bath components in selected metal-making routes. Existing fluorination skills could support their preparation after individual rare earths have been separated. Nd, Pr, Dy and Tb connect particularly to magnets; Gd's inclusion is a chemical adjacency, not a claim that it has identical demand or processing economics.

chemistryList.name: Liquid-liquid extraction and purification (pharma, agrochemicals)
chemistryList.who: India's drug industry (third largest by volume); API makers; Sudeep Pharma.
chemistryList.carries_over_to: Solvent-extraction cascades for rare earths and purified phosphoric acid; high-purity salts.
chemistryList.summary: A reusable separation skill: move selected molecules or metal ions between two liquids, then recover a purified product. India has chemical equipment suppliers and actual mineral-separation operators; transferring pharmaceutical experience to a new mineral still requires a qualified flowsheet.

links.how: The same separation principle applies to the remaining heavy rare earths in the workbook. Each needs a suitable feed and element-specific cascade. Their inclusion here expresses a technology connection, not a claim that India already commercially separates every listed element. A pharmaceutical plant cannot be counted as that capacity.
links.fit: Adjacent; commercial element-by-element Indian coverage unverified

chemistryList.name: Ion-exchange resins
chemistryList.who: Ion Exchange India (Ankleshwar; hydrometallurgy and nuclear-grade resins); HWB-BARC's special resin.
chemistryList.carries_over_to: Gallium from Bayer liquor; scandium; heavy-REE polishing; lithium from brine.
chemistryList.fit: Direct for gallium (demo); adjacent for the rest
chemistryList.summary: Selective resin beads capture dissolved ions, then release them into a cleaner stream. India manufactures resins and has a gallium-recovery demonstration project, but each mineral application needs its own chemistry, feed testing and operating evidence.

links.how: Selective loading, elution and chromatography can concentrate or polish rare-earth fractions and, in designed systems, separate individual elements. The U.S. Bureau of Mines demonstrated heavy-rare-earth separation with sulfonic and chelating resins. Its experimental results are evidence of mechanism, not contemporary Indian industrial capacity for each workbook-linked element.
links.fit: Established separation principle; element-specific Indian scale unverified

chemistryList.name: Hydrometallurgy and process R&D
chemistryList.carries_over_to: Tellurium from slime; nickel from overburden; magnet and battery recycling; REE separation flowsheets.
chemistryList.summary: Hydrometallurgy dissolves and separates elements into useful products. India has process-development experience, pilot facilities and some industrial transfers. That foundation can support several mineral chains; each feed still needs its own validated flowsheet and commercial case.

links.how: These links identify potential applications of separation expertise to heavy rare earths. The reviewed sources do not establish commercial Indian supply of all six. Recovering a mixed rare-earth product still leaves element-by-element separation, yield and customer qualification to demonstrate.
links.fit: Research carry-over; commercial supply not established by these sources
